topics.title: Gender division and women in politics

learn.hook: Who makes the chai at home and who fixes the tap? Many families have unwritten rules — and those rules shape politics too.
points: Gender division is a hierarchical social division based on social expectations and stereotypes, not on biology.

Sexual division of labour: a system in which all work inside the home is done by women of the family, or organised by them through domestic helpers. Women's work at home is often unpaid and not valued, even though many women also work outside.

Women around the world organised and agitated for equal rights — first for the right to vote, then for equal opportunities in education, work and political life. More radical movements that aim at equality in personal and family life too are called feminist movements. In Sweden, Norway and Finland, women's participation in public life is very high.

Patriarchy (literally 'rule by father') is a system that values men more and gives them power over women. In India, problems include lower literacy among women, unequal pay despite the law of equal wages for equal work, a preference for sons that has lowered the child sex ratio, and unsafe public spaces.

Political representation: at least one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women. Women's share in Parliament and state assemblies has been low. The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) reserves about one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, the state legislative assemblies and the Delhi Assembly for women. It takes effect only after the next census and a fresh delimitation of constituencies, so these seats are not reserved yet. Exam tip: older printings of the NCERT book describe this as a bill still pending in Parliament; answer using the wording in your own copy of the textbook.

example.q: Think it through: Why does it matter if very few women sit in the legislature, even though women can vote?
steps: Legislatures make the laws and policies that affect everyone.
If women are poorly represented, issues like safety, equal pay and health may get less attention.
Reserving seats is one way to make sure women's voices are heard where decisions are made.
example.answer: Because representation affects which problems get solved; more women in legislatures helps bring women's concerns into policy.

learn.reallife: Notice how many women sarpanches and councillors now lead villages and towns across India — the one-third reservation in local bodies has made that possible.

games.title: True or false: gender and politics
items: Gender division is based mainly on social expectations and stereotypes, not biology.
The roles given to men and women are shaped by society.
At least one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women.
This has brought many women into local government.
Patriarchy is a system that values women more than men.
Patriarchy values men more and gives them power over women.
Feminist movements aim at equality for women in personal, family and public life.
They seek equal rights and opportunities for women.
The law in India allows employers to pay women less than men for the same work.
The law provides equal wages for equal work, though in practice women are often paid less.
A preference for sons has led to a fall in the child sex ratio in some parts of India.
Sex-selective practices have reduced the number of girls per thousand boys in some areas.

items.text: A system that values men more and gives them power over women is called ___.
Work inside the home done mostly by women is part of the sexual division of ___.
At least ___ of seats in local bodies are reserved for women.
Movements aiming at equality for women are called ___ movements.

quiz.q: What is meant by the 'sexual division of labour'?
options: Men and women doing exactly the same work
Work inside the home is done by women, or organised by them through domestic helpers, while men mostly work outside
A law dividing jobs between men and women
quiz.explain: It is a social system in which household work is seen as women's responsibility.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the division of labour is a legal rule rather than a social practice

quiz.q: What does 'patriarchy' literally mean?
quiz.explain: Patriarchy literally means rule by father; it is a system that gives men power over women.
quiz.mistake: Confuses patriarchy with democracy or matriarchy

quiz.q: What is the main aim of feminist movements?
options: To give women power over men
Equality for women in personal, family and public life
quiz.explain: Feminist movements seek equal rights and opportunities for women, not dominance over men.
quiz.mistake: Misunderstands feminism as wanting women to rule over men

quiz.q: In which group of countries is women's participation in public life very high?
options: Scandinavian countries such as Sweden, Norway and Finland
quiz.explain: In Scandinavian countries women take part in public life at very high levels.
quiz.mistake: Does not know examples of high female participation in public life

quiz.q: What share of seats in panchayats and municipalities is reserved for women?
quiz.explain: At least one-third of the seats in local government bodies are reserved for women.
quiz.mistake: Confuses local body reservation with other figures

quiz.q: Which is a sign that Indian women still face disadvantage despite legal protection?
options: Women are often paid less than men for similar work, even though the law provides equal wages
quiz.explain: The law says equal wages for equal work, but in practice women are often paid less.
quiz.mistake: Mistakes a right that exists for evidence of disadvantage

quiz.q: Why is women's work at home often not recognised?
options: Because it is done only on holidays
Because men do all the housework
Because it is usually unpaid and taken for granted
Because it is banned by law
quiz.explain: Household work is unpaid, so it is often not counted or valued, though it is essential.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only paid work counts as work

quiz.q: In 2023 a constitutional amendment was passed about women's representation. What does it provide?
options: Reservation of one-half of Rajya Sabha seats for women
Voting rights for women for the first time
Reservation of one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for women, after the next census and delimitation
quiz.explain: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 reserves about one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies (and the Delhi Assembly) for women. It applies only after the next census and delimitation. If your NCERT copy calls it a pending bill, use the textbook's wording in the board exam.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with voting rights, which Indian women have had since the Constitution came into force

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Why do people say gender is a political issue? Isn't it just about home?'
teach.praise: Chirp! From housework to the legislature, gender equality needs politics — and reservation helps women's voices count!
teach.nudge: Good! What is patriarchy, and how does reservation help women in politics?

topics.title: Religion, communalism and the secular state

learn.hook: India is home to many faiths — Diwali lamps, Eid sweets, Christmas stars and Gurpurab langars. How does democracy keep this harmony?
points: Religion and politics: Gandhiji said religion can never be separated from politics — by religion he meant the moral values common to all religions, not any one faith. People may express their needs and interests in politics as members of a religious community.

Communalism is the problem: when one religion's beliefs are presented as superior, when the demands of one religious group are formed in opposition to another, and when state power is used to establish the domination of one religious group.

Forms of communalism: everyday beliefs and stereotypes about other religions; a desire for political dominance of one's own community (or a separate political unit); political mobilisation on religious lines using sacred symbols and emotional appeals; and, at its ugliest, communal violence. India saw terrible communal violence at the time of Partition.

India is a secular state: there is no official religion (unlike Sri Lanka, whose constitution gives a special place to Buddhism); everyone is free to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not follow any; and discrimination on grounds of religion is prohibited.
The Constitution also allows the state to intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities — for example, it bans untouchability.

example.q: Think it through: A leader tells voters, 'Vote only for people of your own religion, because the other community is against you.' Is this communalism?
steps: The message presents one religious group's interests as opposed to another's.
It uses religious identity to mobilise votes and spreads distrust.
Expressing needs as a community is allowed; setting communities against each other is communalism.
example.answer: Yes. It is communal politics, because it builds hostility between religious groups for political gain.

learn.reallife: When your school celebrates Holi, Eid, Christmas and Guru Nanak Jayanti together, it reflects the spirit of a secular state that treats all faiths with equal respect.

games.title: Secular practice or communalism?
items: No official religion for the state
Freedom to follow any religion or none
Banning untouchability to ensure equality
Using state power to dominate other religious groups
Spreading stereotypes about another religion
Asking for votes by creating fear of another community
No discrimination on grounds of religion

games.title: Match the idea
pairs: One religion presented as superior to others
Gandhiji's view of religion in politics
Moral values common to all religions
Profess, practise and propagate any faith

quiz.q: What did Gandhiji mean when he said religion can never be separated from politics?
options: Politics should be run by priests
One religion should be the state religion
Politics should be guided by the moral values common to all religions
Religious festivals should be government holidays
quiz.explain: By religion Gandhiji meant ethical values from all religions, not any particular faith.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Gandhiji wanted a religious state

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of communalism?
options: Celebrating festivals of many religions together
Presenting the beliefs of one religion as superior to those of others
quiz.explain: Communalism treats one religion as superior and sets religious groups against each other.
quiz.mistake: Confuses practising a religion with communalism

quiz.q: Which is a feature of India as a secular state?
quiz.explain: India has no official religion and treats all religions with equal respect.
quiz.mistake: Thinks secularism means banning religion

quiz.q: Why does the Constitution allow the state to intervene in religious matters in some cases?
options: To ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability
To close all places of worship
quiz.explain: The state may intervene to protect equality, such as by banning untouchability.
quiz.mistake: Thinks secularism means the state can never act on religious matters

quiz.q: Which country's constitution gives a special place to Buddhism, unlike India?
quiz.explain: Sri Lanka's constitution says the state shall protect and foster Buddhism; India has no official religion.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the Sri Lanka case from the power-sharing chapter

quiz.q: Using sacred symbols, religious leaders and emotional appeals to bring followers of one religion together in politics is called:
quiz.explain: This is one of the forms communalism takes in politics.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise religious mobilisation as a form of communalism

quiz.q: Which statement about religion and politics is correct?
options: People can never raise demands as members of a religious community
Every connection between religion and politics is communal
Religion and politics must be completely separate in every sense
People may express interests as members of a religious community, but using religion to set groups against each other is communalism
quiz.explain: Expressing needs as a community is acceptable; the problem is when religion becomes the basis for hostility and domination.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any mention of religion in politics is communal

quiz.q: Which of these is a freedom guaranteed by India's Constitution?
options: Freedom to force others to change their religion
Freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not to follow any
Freedom to discriminate on religious grounds
quiz.explain: Every citizen is free to profess, practise and propagate any religion or none.
quiz.mistake: Misreads freedom of religion as freedom to discriminate or coerce

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'What is communalism, and how does India stay secular? Explain kindly!'
teach.praise: Chirp! Respect every faith, no official religion and no hostility — that's secular India!
teach.nudge: Nice! Can you say what makes something communal, and two features of a secular state?

learn.hook: Caste can shape politics, and politics can reshape caste. It's a two-way street!
points: Caste division is special to India: occupations were passed down hereditarily, people married within their caste, and some groups faced exclusion and untouchability.

Social reformers such as Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker worked for a society without caste inequality. Urbanisation, literacy, education and occupational mobility have weakened old caste rules, and the Constitution prohibits caste-based discrimination.

Caste in politics: parties consider the caste composition of voters when choosing candidates; parties and candidates may appeal to caste sentiment; universal adult franchise made leaders mobilise all groups; and it gave dalits and backward castes a sense of political voice.

But elections are not only about caste: no parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste; no party wins all the votes of a caste; many voters have no candidate from their caste; and ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose. Voters also judge performance, leaders and party policies.

Politics in caste: each caste group tries to grow by including neighbouring castes, forms coalitions with others, and new groupings like 'backward' and 'forward' castes emerge. Caste still links with economic status: on average upper castes are better off, while dalits and adivasis are worse off.

example.q: Think it through: A party picks a candidate of the largest caste in a constituency. Is it sure to win?
steps: No constituency has a clear majority of one caste, so one caste alone cannot decide the result.
No party gets all the votes of any one caste.
Voters also weigh the government's work, the leaders and the parties' policies.
example.answer: No. Caste matters, but no candidate can win on caste votes alone.

learn.reallife: In any election season, you can read news about parties discussing which communities live in a constituency — and also about the issues voters care about, like roads, water and jobs.

games.title: Caste in politics or politics in caste?
items: Parties choose candidates keeping in mind the caste of voters
Candidates appeal to caste sentiment for support
A caste group includes neighbouring castes to become bigger
Caste groups form coalitions with other castes
New groups like 'backward' and 'forward' castes emerge
Universal adult franchise makes leaders seek support from all groups

games.title: True or false: caste and elections
items: Every parliamentary constituency in India has a clear majority of one caste.
No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste.
The Constitution prohibits caste-based discrimination.
It also abolished untouchability.
Ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose elections in India.
This shows voters judge performance, not only caste.
Urbanisation and education have weakened old caste rules.
Mixing in cities, schools and offices has loosened caste barriers.
One party can be sure of getting all the votes of a caste.
No party wins the votes of all the voters of any caste.
Caste no longer has any link with economic status in India.
On average, upper castes remain better off, while dalits and adivasis are worse off.

quiz.q: Which of these reformers worked to end caste inequality?
quiz.explain: Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker are among those who worked against caste discrimination.
quiz.mistake: Does not recall the social reformers linked with the anti-caste struggle

quiz.q: Which factor has helped weaken old caste rules in India?
quiz.explain: City life, education and new kinds of jobs have broken down many old caste barriers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks caste rules are unchanged since earlier times

quiz.q: Which statement shows that elections are NOT only about caste?
options: Parties consider caste when choosing candidates
No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste
quiz.explain: Since no caste is a clear majority anywhere, candidates must win the support of many groups.
quiz.mistake: Picks a point that shows caste in politics rather than its limits

quiz.q: How did universal adult franchise affect caste in politics?
options: It allowed only upper castes to vote
It removed the vote from dalits
It made leaders seek support from all groups and gave a political voice to groups that were once neglected
quiz.explain: When every adult can vote, leaders must mobilise all groups, including those that were earlier excluded.
quiz.mistake: Misunderstands universal adult franchise

quiz.q: When a caste group includes neighbouring castes to become bigger and stronger politically, it is an example of:
quiz.explain: Politics changes caste groups themselves — that is 'politics in caste'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'caste in politics' with 'politics in caste'

quiz.q: Why do ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose elections in India?
options: Because voters also judge performance, leaders and policies
Because elections are not held regularly
quiz.explain: If caste alone decided results, those in power would rarely lose; voters also weigh how well the government did.
quiz.mistake: Assumes voters choose only on the basis of caste

quiz.q: What does the Constitution of India say about caste-based discrimination?
options: It allows it in private jobs
quiz.explain: The Constitution prohibits caste-based discrimination and abolished untouchability.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the constitutional position on caste

quiz.q: Which statement about caste and economic status is correct, according to the textbook?
options: All castes now have exactly equal incomes
Dalits and adivasis are on average better off than upper castes
Caste has nothing to do with poverty
On average, upper castes are better off, while dalits and adivasis are worse off
quiz.explain: Caste continues to be linked with economic status, though every caste has both rich and poor people.
quiz.mistake: Thinks caste inequality has completely disappeared

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Do people vote only by caste? Explain how caste and politics affect each other!'
teach.praise: Chirp! Caste shapes politics, politics reshapes caste — but voters judge much more than caste!
teach.nudge: Good start! Why can't caste alone decide an election? And how does politics change caste groups?
